newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Thomson says torrid acquisition pace to cool.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Thomson says torrid acquisition pace to cool.

text.p: The rapid pace of acquisitions by Canadian publishing and travel firm Thomson Corp. is likely to slow as the company digests its recent purchases, president and chief executive Michael Brown told Reuters.

"In the future you will find that our acquisition spending will be much more normal and much more tactical than it has been in the past," Brown, the man behind the recent $3.4 billion takeover of Eagan, Minn.-based legal publisher West Publishing, said in an interview this week.
He said that Toronto-based Thomson was gobbling up companies last year at the rate of one a week.
"We are not proactively seeking a major strategic acquisition at the moment. But if something comes up unsolicited, we've got to look at it and respond," Brown said.
"I think where we would most like to see acquisitions ... where we see the perhaps the greatest change and fastest growth are in financial services and healthcare."
The West deal sparked criticism from rivals in the industry. Last week, the Lexis-Nexis arm of Anglo-Dutch publishing company Reed Elsevier filed suit in a U.S. district court opposing the deal.
Brown and other Thomson executives dismissed the suit as without merit.
"The words I have read from them seem to indicate that they have made a really bad job of buying Lexis-Nexis ... They're showing desperation," he said.
The West deal has been approved by the U.S. Justice Department, which asked Thomson to shed 70 products the department valued at about $275 million.

Brown said: "We are right on our expectations (for West). I don't see any disappointment at all next year and if you look out to the ... expectations we have for the year 2000, I think we are going to deliver on maybe plus a bit more too."

Many U.S. analysts, galvanised by the acquisition of West and the fact that 75 percent of Thomson's profits come from the United States, have been wondering when a New York Stock Exchange listing might be in the works.

Brown said there are no immediate plans to seek a spot on the Big Board, but added: "I can see us sometime in the future getting a New York quote. I suppose if you look at our evolution ... maybe getting a New York listing one day is like growing up."
Brown, 61, who plans to retire next year after more than a decade as president, has moved Thomson into speciality and professional publishing from cyclical, advertising-dependent newspapers.
But he added that the analysts clamouring for the sale of the travel group, seen as an odd fit in the increasingly focused conglomerate, will need to wait a while.

"While travel isn't for sale, we have had offers. We have rejected them all. And the fact is, the business today is worth massively more than it was 10 years ago ... so we were right to keep it," Brown said.

"You look at the logic and see that right out in the dim distant future, the business will come apart. But short-term I have got to say ... we have no intention right now of selling that business," he added.
He said the divestment of a big part of the newspaper group was mostly complete, although a few more papers may go on the block before the end of the year.
But Thomson's flagship paper, Toronto's Globe and Mail, will never hit the block, Brown said.
